 El Niño warning: What Kenyans need to know as heavy rains loom
 Friday 06th November, 2026 07:05 PM | 
 By Sharon Atieno 
 Flooding caused by El Niño rains. 
 El Niño is a climate phenomenon that can influence rainfall patterns and increase the risk of flooding in Kenya. As the country moves deeper into the October-December short-rains season, forecasts of above-average rainfall have raised expectations of heavier rains, even as hot daytime conditions persist in several areas.
 The Kenya Meteorological Service forecast above-average rainfall in 43 counties in its November 2026 monthly outlook released on October 30, 2026. The counties include Nairobi, Mombasa, Kisumu, Nakuru, Kiambu, Machakos and Kajiado.
 However, the anticipated rains do not mean every part of the country will experience continuous rainfall. Understanding El Niño, its possible effects and the importance of preparation is crucial as the season progresses.
 What is El Niño?
 El Niño occurs when sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean become warmer than normal, influencing atmospheric circulation and weather patterns across the world.
 In East Africa, El Niño conditions have historically been associated with enhanced rainfall during the October-December season. The additional rain can replenish water sources, improve soil moisture and support agricultural production.
 However, excessive rainfall can also cause flash floods, landslides, soil erosion and damage to homes, roads and crops. The effects depend on the strength of the climate event, local conditions and other weather systems.
 Why hot weather persists despite rain forecasts
 The continued sunshine in parts of Kenya does not necessarily mean the seasonal rainfall forecast has failed. Rainfall can vary considerably between counties, with some areas receiving showers while neighbouring locations remain dry.
 In its November 2026 outlook, the Kenya Meteorological Service forecast warmer-than-average temperatures across the country alongside above-average rainfall in several counties.
 This means Kenyans may experience hot afternoons followed by showers or thunderstorms rather than continuous cold and cloudy conditions. The amount and timing of rainfall also depend on atmospheric circulation, moisture availability and other climate systems, including the Indian Ocean Dipole.
 State of roads in Kitengela town following the past heavy rains. PHOTO/Christine Musa 
 In an interview published on October 22, 2026 Kenya Meteorological Department Director of Public Weather Services Hannah Kimani explained t hat low-pressure systems developing over the northern Indian Ocean had temporarily slowed the southward movement of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), which plays an important role in Kenya’s seasonal rainfall.
 “During October to December, the Intertropical Convergence Zone brings us rainfall when it is moving from the north to the southern hemisphere,” she said.
 The disruption contributed to uneven rainfall distribution, with some areas receiving rain earlier than others.
 Counties facing possible flood risks
 The November outlook identified Nairobi, Kiambu, Nakuru, Nyeri, Murang’a, Machakos, Kajiado, Mombasa, Kilifi, Kisumu, Kakamega, Kisii, Bungoma, Busia, Meru and Embu among counties expected to receive above-average rainfall.
 Low-lying settlements, flood-prone river basins, urban areas with inadequate drainage and steep highland locations may face increased risks of flooding and landslides.
 For farmers, improved rainfall could support crop growth and replenish water sources. However, excessive rain may cause waterlogging, crop diseases, soil erosion and disruptions to the transportation of farm produce.
 How Kenyans can prepare
 Residents should monitor official weather alerts, clear drainage channels and avoid crossing flooded roads or rivers. Households in flood-prone areas should identify safer routes and evacuation points.
 Farmers should seek advice from agricultural extension officers on planting schedules, drainage and soil conservation.
 As the short-rains season progresses, Kenyans should follow the Kenya Meteorological Service’s daily, five-day and seven-day forecasts. Although November is expected to bring improved rainfall distribution, the timing and intensity of rain will vary across the country.
 The key message is that hot weather does not rule out heavy rainfall. Early preparation and attention to local forecasts can help communities reduce the risks associated with possible floods while taking advantage of the benefits of the rainy season.
